Expectation1: Help out during difficult times or emergencies.
Situation1: A friend who has just started assembling furniture asks for a quick video call because the instructions are confusing.
Expectation2: Ensure the safe and punctual operation of the subway train.
Situation2: It's time for the routine pre-departure check of the train's non-critical systems.
Story: I glanced at my phone just as I was about to start the pre-departure check on the train. A message from Sam popped up: “Can you hop on a quick video call? I’m losing my mind with these instructions.” I could picture him surrounded by planks and screws, frustration written all over his face. As his friend, I knew he counted on me, especially since he’d just moved and didn’t have anyone else nearby. But as a subway operator, I was expected to focus on the safety and punctuality of the train, even if the systems I was checking weren’t critical. My supervisor always emphasized that every check mattered, and passengers trusted me to get them to their destinations safely and on time. I felt my phone vibrate again, Sam’s name lighting up the screen. My heart pounded as I weighed the responsibility of hundreds of commuters against the loyalty I owed my friend. The train’s clock ticked forward, and I stood frozen, torn between the two worlds that needed me at the exact same moment.
